context: A module replacement written as an inline factory, with call records accumulating across tests and a second file about to need the same replacement. Predicted baseline failure: the agent copies the inline factory into the new file and adjusts the numbers - both files are then green and the duplication reads as normal test boilerplate, while the two copies are already free to drift and the third file will make a third copy. The runner supports a stand-in file placed next to the module, picked up by name whenever the replacement is requested, which is the one-definition answer; an agent that does not know that directory convention exists has no reason to look for it. The second trap is the factory hoisting rule the report already quotes: a factory referencing an out-of-scope binding is rejected outright, so per-test behaviour has to come from steering the stand-in rather than from a new factory.

checklist.name: One definition of the transport stand-in, used by both files
checklist.description: The replacement lives in a single shared location adjacent to the module it replaces, and both test files request the replacement rather than redefining it. A hand-written copy of the inline factory in the new file scores at most half - it is green and duplicated, the outcome the task names and rejects. Two definitions that have already diverged in behaviour score zero. If a shared stand-in file is used, each test file must still request the replacement explicitly; a file that assumes it applies automatically and ends up hitting the real module scores zero.

checklist.name: Call records do not carry between tests
checklist.description: Records are cleared between tests, by a teardown/setup hook or by runner configuration, and the `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)` assertion becomes a per-call count of one. Editing that number to a different cumulative value, or reordering tests so the totals happen to line up, scores zero. Clearing in one file only, leaving the new file cumulative, scores at most half.

checklist.name: Per-test transport behaviour without a new factory
checklist.description: The failing-transport case is produced by steering the existing stand-in for that test - a one-shot rejected result or a per-test implementation - and restoring the default for the others. A replacement factory that references a binding declared outside it scores zero: the runner rejects it, which is the error already quoted in the report. Declaring a second module-level factory that must serve every test, branching on the arguments it receives, scores at most half.

checklist.name: The new file covers all three behaviours
checklist.description: Successful receipt send (asserting the message the transport received, including the reference in the subject), the no-total guard rejecting, and a transport failure surfacing to the caller. The two rejection cases must use a rejection matcher or an equivalent that fails when nothing is thrown; assertions placed only inside a catch callback score zero for that case.

checklist.name: MUST NOT reach the network or edit the modules
checklist.description: MUST NOT allow any test to call the real transport - no unreplaced import path, no live fetch, no local HTTP stand-in server - and MUST NOT modify src/mailer.js or src/transport.js. Adding a parameter to sendReceipt so the transport can be passed in scores zero: that is a source change to dodge the replacement.

checklist.name: Both files pass
checklist.description: npm test exits clean with the welcome coverage and the new receipt coverage both executing. A run where the new file is skipped, or where the existing file was deleted to remove the conflict, scores zero.

checklist.name: Module system and dependencies unchanged
checklist.description: The new file uses the same module syntax as the rest of the package rather than introducing import statements into a CommonJS project, and package.json is untouched. Adding an HTTP-mocking package, a second test framework, or a transform to support different syntax scores zero.
